articles.title: All or Nothing: Testing DynamoDB Transaction Atomicity with Tables
articles.excerpt: What a four-operation failure taught me about commits, cancellation reasons, and verifying that nothing was written. A database transaction is easy to appreciate when it succeeds. The more important q…
articles.body: What a four-operation failure taught me about commits, cancellation reasons, and verifying that nothing was written. A database transaction is easy to appreciate when it succeeds. The more important question is what happens when one operation fails after several other changes have been requested. Suppose an application needs to create a record, update an existing balance, and delete an obsolete item. If a final validation check fails, none of those changes should be committed. Otherwise, the application could be left with data that describes a transaction that never actually completed. I tested this behavior using Tables by ServerlessCreed and Amazon DynamoDB .

articles.title: Chemical precipitation is a pH window, not a setpoint
articles.excerpt: The caustic dose in a metal-finishing plant is usually governed by a single number: the pH that met the copper limit the last time anyone ran a full analysis. That number is right often enough to beco…
articles.body: The caustic dose in a metal-finishing plant is usually governed by a single number: the pH that met the copper limit the last time anyone ran a full analysis. That number is right often enough to become policy, and wrong in exactly the hours when a chelating agent, an ammonia load, or an amphoteric metal moves the real solubility curve away from it. Applies generally; the one jurisdiction-specific remark below is labelled as Korean. The lever is solubility, not alkalinity Hydroxide precipitation looks like a dosing problem because the actuator is a pump. Chemically it is a solubility problem: metal leaves the water only to the extent the equilibrium allows, and hydroxide solubility is a curve with a minimum, not a monotonic response to more caustic.

articles.title: Keeping High-Risk Incident Runbooks Accurate as Infrastructure Evolves
articles.excerpt: Anatomy of a Stale Runbook and the Cost of Blind Trust Operational runbooks for high-risk procedures—such as regional failovers, database restores, and certificate rotations—inevitably decay because t…
articles.body: Anatomy of a Stale Runbook and the Cost of Blind Trust Operational runbooks for high-risk procedures—such as regional failovers, database restores, and certificate rotations—inevitably decay because they attempt to model a living, mutating system through static, unlinked prose. As infrastructure evolves through rapid pull requests, Terraform infrastructure-as-code merges, and IAM policy updates, a persistent change-propagation gap opens between runtime reality and documentation stored in remote wikis. When a service owner updates an API endpoint, renames a message queue, or shifts a database schema, the live system state changes instantaneously, while the documentation text remains frozen.

articles.title: SQL Server to BigQuery: Build a CDC Pipeline That Lands in Your Own Bucket
articles.excerpt: A SQL Server to BigQuery job often begins life as a nightly bcp export, a CSV file in a bucket and a bq load. That is enough for a dashboard refreshed once a day. It stops being enough when an order s…
articles.body: A SQL Server to BigQuery job often begins life as a nightly bcp export, a CSV file in a bucket and a bq load . That is enough for a dashboard refreshed once a day. It stops being enough when an order ships at noon, a customer moves city, and the afternoon report still shows the morning's values. SQL Server already records those changes. With change data capture (CDC) on, the SQL Server Agent copies each insert, update and delete from the transaction log into a change table. What is left to decide is who reads those tables and where the rows land. The usual options: Datastream for SQL Server : Google's managed CDC service, near real time by Google's description. Nothing to run, and the rows land in native BigQuery datasets that only BigQuery reads.

The companies said that their initial scope will center on design and feasibility, as well as technology integration.

articles.title: Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still
articles.excerpt: The queen in the northern night sky is supposedly one of the easiest constellations to recognize — you just look for a W. Or is that an M?
articles.body: Some constellations are like old friends. You know them well, they're always there, and they never seem to change. A case in point is Cassiopeia, the queen. Its beautiful name comes from Greek mythology — the mother of Andromeda — and its shape is said to represent a queen sitting on a throne. To a stargazer, Cassiopeia is best known as a prominent northern constellation shaped like the letter W. It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting. It's so often a signpost, not a destination. But look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 27, 1885: Astronomer captures 1st known photo of a meteor during an Andromedid meteor storm
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor. The picture was taken by Austro-Hungarian astronomer Ladislaus Weinek. He captured the trail of the meteor on a photographic plate in the Czech Republic. The meteor he captured was part of the Andromedid meteor shower . The Andromedids were associated with Biela's Comet , which broke apart in the 1850s. When Weinek observed the meteor shower in 1885, it was in the middle of a meteor storm . This means that there were way more meteors than usual. Skywatchers could see thousands of meteors per hour. The November 1872 incidence of the Andromedid meteor shower, as seen over France, in a painting.
